Empirical Research Plan  
“Immigration and Native Labor‐Market Outcomes in the United States, 1960–1990”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) difference-in-differences (a “shift–share” or “Bartik” instrument).

Rationale  
• Immigration is not randomly assigned across local labor markets; immigrant workers tend to move where labor demand is strong, biasing OLS.  
• A shift–share IV exploits the fact that immigrants from any particular origin country disproportionately settle in the same U.S. localities where earlier migrants from that origin already live (network effects). Historical enclave shares (the “shares”) interact with nationwide origin-specific inflows in later decades (the “shifts”) to generate plausibly exogenous, differential predicted inflows across regions over time.  
• The panel structure (1960, 1970, 1980, 1990) allows a DID interpretation once region and decade fixed effects are included.  
• No discontinuity or hard cutoff exists, so RDD is infeasible; event study graphs will, however, be used to probe dynamic effects and pre-trends.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
ImmShare_rt = Immigrants_rt / LaborForce_rt  
= fraction of the labor force in region r, decade t, that is foreign born.

Control group / counterfactual  
Regions with lower immigrant shares at time t serve as the control. The identifying variation is continuous; regions receive different “doses” of treatment.

Instrument (first-stage predictor)  
PredImmShare_rt = (Σ_o BaseShare_r,o,1970 × NatImmFlow_o,t) / LaborForce_rt  
where  
• BaseShare_r,o,1970 = immigrant share from origin o residing in region r in 1970 (pre-period).  
• NatImmFlow_o,t = total national inflow of immigrants from origin o between decades t-1 and t.  
Treatment timing  
Decennial observations 1960→1970→1980→1990. The “event” is the decade-specific immigrant inflow. All regions are observed before and after, but with heterogeneous intensity.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Historical enclave shares strongly predict later decade-by-origin inflows. Plausible and testable (first-stage F-stat > 10).  
A2. Exclusion – Conditional on region and year fixed effects and controls, historical shares affect native wages/employment only via contemporaneous immigrant inflows. Plausible because 1970 enclave patterns are predetermined relative to later labor-demand shocks, but threatened if shocks are persistent (see threats section).  
A3. No differential pre-trends – Absent immigration, native outcomes in high-enclave and low-enclave regions would have followed parallel trends. Event-study coefficients on pre-1970 decades should be ≈0.  
A4. Stable labor-market definition – Workers primarily compete within commuting zones; mobility across CZs is limited within a decade. Literature suggests most migration is within rather than across CZs; still, some violation possible.  
A5. SUTVA – Immigrant inflows into one region do not directly affect native wages in another (no large spillovers). Reasonable given localized labor markets.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous local demand shocks correlated with enclave size.  
   – Add region-specific linear time trends.  
   – Control for lagged industry composition × decade fixed effects.  
   – Use a “leave-one-out” version of the instrument (exclude own region when computing national flows).  

T2. Selective native out-migration (“resiorting”) in response to immigrants.  
   – Estimate effect on both resident natives and “stayers” (those present in two consecutive censuses).  
   – Instrument remains valid if migration is a channel, but interpret results as local-labor-market perspective.  

T3. Measurement error in immigrant counts.  
   – IV attenuates classical error, but still run robustness with ACS sample weights and alternative immigrant definitions (foreign-born vs. non-citizen).  

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # feols/iv_robust
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume individual-level census files already cleaned & appended
# Each file has variables: cz, year, wage, employed, native, foreign_born,
# country_of_birth (coo), personal_weight

census <- fread("census_1960_1990.csv")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Collapse to CZ × year cells for native workers
cz_year <- census[native == 1,
  .(
    wage_native   = weighted.mean(wage,  personal_weight, na.rm=TRUE),
    emp_rate      = weighted.mean(employed, personal_weight),
    labor_force   = sum(personal_weight),
    immigrants    = 0 # placeholder
  ),
  by = .(cz, year)]

# Add immigrant counts
imm_counts <- census[foreign_born == 1,
  .(immigrants = sum(personal_weight)), by = .(cz, year)]
cz_year <- merge(cz_year, imm_counts, by = c("cz", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
cz_year[is.na(immigrants), immigrants := 0]

# Immigrant share
cz_year[, imm_share := immigrants / labor_force]

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Build Shift–Share Instrument
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# a. Base shares (1970)
base <- census[year == 1970 & foreign_born == 1,
      .(base_count = sum(personal_weight)), by = .(cz, coo)]
total_base_cz <- base[, .(tot = sum(base_count)), by = cz]
base <- merge(base, total_base_cz, by = "cz")
base[, base_share := base_count / tot]

# b. National inflows by origin and decade
nat_flows <- census[foreign_born == 1 & year %in% c(1960, 1970, 1980, 1990),
      .(nat_stock = sum(personal_weight)), by = .(year, coo)]
setorder(nat_flows, coo, year)
nat_flows[, nat_inflow := nat_stock - shift(nat_stock), by = coo]

# Keep inflows for 1970, 1980, 1990 (using prior decade stock difference)
nat_inflow_dec <- nat_flows[!is.na(nat_inflow) & year != 1960,
                            .(year, coo, nat_inflow)]

# c. Predicted inflow per CZ × year
pred_list <- merge(base, nat_inflow_dec, by = "coo", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
pred_list[, pred_imm := base_share * nat_inflow]
pred_cz <- pred_list[, .(pred_imm = sum(pred_imm)), by = .(cz, year)]

# Merge into main
cz_year <- merge(cz_year, pred_cz, by = c("cz", "year"), all.x = TRUE)
cz_year[is.na(pred_imm), pred_imm := 0]
cz_year[, pred_imm_share := pred_imm / labor_force]

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main 2SLS Regression
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Baseline: native log wages on immigrant share (instrumented)
cz_year[, ln_wage := log(wage_native)]

iv_spec <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ imm_share | cz + year | (imm_share ~ pred_imm_share),
  data = cz_year, se = "hetero"
)
summary(iv_spec)

# Panel with native employment rate as outcome
iv_emp <- feols(
  emp_rate ~ imm_share | cz + year | (imm_share ~ pred_imm_share),
  data = cz_year, se = "hetero"
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Leave-one-out instrument
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Recompute nat_inflow excluding CZ’s own contribution
# (for brevity, pseudo-code; implementation similar using data.table joins)

# Robustness regression
iv_spec_lo <- feols(
  ln_wage ~ imm_share | cz + year | (imm_share ~ pred_imm_share_LOO),
  data = cz_year, se = "hetero"
)

# Compare coefficients
etable(list(Main = iv_spec, LeaveOneOut = iv_spec_lo), se.below = TRUE)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory offers ambiguous predictions—immigrants can both compete with and complement natives. Prior literature tends to find small to modest negative wage effects for less-skilled natives and near-zero effects overall. My prior: a 1-percentage-point increase in immigrant share lowers average native wages by roughly 0.3% (elasticity ≈ −0.03) and reduces native employment 0.05–0.1 pp. Heterogeneous impacts likely larger for high-school dropouts (≈ −1%). 

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
C1: Strong first-stage relevance ........................... 1  
C2: Instrument excludability (no direct effect) ............ 0.5  
C3: No differential pre-trends / parallel trends ........... 0.8  
C4: Limited spillovers across regions (SUTVA) .............. 0.7  
C5: Correct standard-error clustering (CZ level) ........... 1  

Total ≈ 4 / 5; overall credibility: good but not bullet-proof.

------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers a transparent, empirically rigorous framework to estimate the causal impact of immigration on native labor-market outcomes using long-run U.S. census data.
